issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is difficult to justify clinically here because the profile contains no Negative Appraisal items and the formulation marks Negative Appraisals as inactive with no links to other active nodes. This item introduces a strong appraisal theme that is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile.

issues.item: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: Avoiding driving or being a passenger in a vehicle is not well grounded by the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items center on sensory re-experiencing, confinement/safety, and startle, but nothing suggests a vehicle-related trauma cue. For terrorism this could occur, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the other selected items and from the inactive Triggers network.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal items and no other selected items suggesting guilt, responsibility, or moral injury; for a terrorism trauma this item can occur, but here it feels clinically disconnected from the rest of the presentation.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Door/window checking is a poor fit with the rest of the threat profile and trauma context. The other threat items suggest generalized hypervigilance/startle and restricted safety, but no trigger, memory, or appraisal content links the terrorism trauma to home-intrusion fear or lock-checking specifically. This makes the item feel mismatched to the formulation and selected symptoms.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened

For a terrorism trauma this could occur, but here the rest of the profile centers on generalized hyperarousal and sensory memory rather than transport-related danger, making this item insufficiently supported and cross-node inconsistent.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: Self-blame is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile. The other endorsed items center on sensory trauma memories and current threat/hypervigilance after terrorism, but there are no Negative Appraisal items supporting a guilt/responsibility theme, and the formulation leaves Negative Appraisals inactive. In this profile, repeated self-blame stands out as an isolated process that is not linked to the active Memory↔Threat pattern and is therefore clinically incoherent relative to the selected items and formulation.

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe a classic sensory re-experiencing / hypervigilance pattern after terrorism, but self-blame, avoiding driving, and avoiding conflict introduce themes that are not represented in the memory or threat content and therefore do not cohere well with the active Memory↔Threat formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, the selected items point in three quite different directions: moral/self-evaluative coping (self-blame), transport-specific avoidance (driving/passenger), and interpersonal avoidance (conflict). This breadth is not impossible, but here it lacks supporting trigger, appraisal, or memory content to connect them into one coherent terrorism-related syndrome.

vignette:
At seventy-two, Tranh had spent decades moving toward danger. As a refugee aid worker, he had walked into bombed-out villages, negotiated with armed militias, and pulled survivors from rubble. But nothing in those years prepared him for the morning the market square in his own city became a war zone. He had been buying fruit when the first explosion came from the café, a sound so close it seemed to enter his chest before his ears registered it. Then the second blast, closer still, and the screaming, and the smell of dust and something else he could not name. He had pressed himself against a concrete planter, watching pieces of a metal chair spin through the air, and he had thought, with terrible clarity, this is how it ends. He survived physically unscathed, but something in him had been torn loose.

In the months that followed, Tranh found that the memory refused to settle. It arrived not as a story he could tell, but as images that seized him without warning: the red of a child’s sandal lying alone in the dust, the white of a man’s eyes as he fell. Sometimes he heard it too—the particular pitch of the first blast, a sound that seemed to vibrate behind his teeth. The memory felt so extreme, so distant from the ordinary life he had once known, that he sometimes struggled to believe it had actually happened to him. He would catch himself staring at his own hands, wondering if they belonged to the same man who had been buying fruit that morning. When these images and sounds surfaced, he found himself replaying what he could have done differently—if he had walked faster, if he had warned someone, if he had chosen a different stall. He blamed himself for not seeing it coming, for being in the wrong place, for surviving when others did not. The self-blame became a loop he could not exit: the memory triggered the rumination, and the rumination made the memory feel more vivid, more present, more impossible to escape.

The memories also changed how he moved through the world. Every ordinary sound now carried the potential of that first blast. A car backfiring, a door slamming, a dropped tray in a restaurant—each one sent a jolt through his body, his heart hammering before his mind could catch up. He became hypervigilant in ways that exhausted him, scanning every street corner, every rooftop, every parked vehicle for signs of threat. The images from the market square would flash through his mind in these moments, as if his brain were reminding him what could happen, what had happened, what would happen again if he let his guard down. He came to believe that safety was an illusion, that danger was always waiting, and that only a very few places—his bedroom, his wife’s car, the back office of the aid agency—offered any real protection.

Tranh stopped driving. Being a passenger was worse; he would grip the door handle, brace for impact, and find himself scanning the road for abandoned bags or parked vans. He also began avoiding any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation—he stopped visiting his brother, stopped attending community meetings, stopped arguing with his wife about even small things. Conflict, he had come to believe, could escalate unpredictably, and he could not afford to be caught off guard again. His wife noticed. She asked why he would not talk to her about the bills, about their son’s visit, about anything. He told her he was just tired. But what he could not say was that every conversation felt like a minefield, and that the memory of the market square made him certain he would not survive another explosion—whether of sound or of anger.
